subject: Coffee & Tea
title: The Boston Tea Party
description: A fast breakdown of The Boston Tea Party for builders.

hook.text: On December 16, 1773, American colonists dumped 342 chests of British tea into Boston Harbor—igniting a revolution.

buildup.text: Britain taxed tea without colonial representation. The tax wasn't huge, but the principle of control enraged colonists.

discovery.text: Disguised as Mohawk Indians, about 100 men boarded three ships and destroyed 46 tons of tea worth £10,000 (millions today).

twist.text: After the protest, drinking tea became unpatriotic. Americans switched to coffee—a shift that persists 250 years later.

climax.text: The Boston Tea Party was the spark for the American Revolution. A beverage tax helped create a nation.

punchline.text: 342 chests of tea, one harbor, a new nation. Coffee became America's patriotic drink.

quiz.question: How did the Boston Tea Party affect American beverage culture?
options: Drinking tea became unpatriotic — Americans switched to coffee

details.summary: In 1773, American colonists dumped 342 chests of British tea into Boston Harbor to protest taxation without representation. The event made drinking tea unpatriotic in America and helped shift the nation toward coffee as its preferred caffeinated beverage for centuries to come.
details.whyItMatters: The Boston Tea Party transformed a beverage preference into a political statement, permanently shaping America's identity as a coffee-drinking rather than tea-drinking nation.
takeaways: Colonists destroyed 342 chests of tea in Boston Harbor in 1773
Drinking tea became unpatriotic in revolutionary America
Coffee replaced tea as America's national caffeinated drink

faq.question: How much tea was destroyed during the Boston Tea Party?
faq.answer: Approximately 342 chests containing about 46 tons of tea worth around 1.7 million dollars in today's money were dumped into the harbor. It was East India Company tea, specifically targeted for the tax it carried.

faq.question: Did America immediately switch from tea to coffee after the Boston Tea Party?
faq.answer: The shift was gradual but culturally driven. Patriotic Americans rejected tea as a symbol of British oppression, and coffeehouses became meeting places for revolutionary planning. Coffee's dominance solidified over the following decades.
